pl-l3d11c2-d1e114.summary: Recalls that Arius's perfidy was to confess Christ a creature; for this his bowels were poured out and he burst asunder, fallen on his face, defiled in the mouth with which he had denied Christ.
claims: Arius taught that Christ is a creature.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e123.summary: Concludes from these testimonies that Christ should not be confessed simply to be made or a creature, but rightly with a qualification, as 'made according to the flesh' or 'according to the man', so that being made is attributed to the humanity, not to God.
claims: Christ is made only according to the flesh or according to the man.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e126.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Trinitate I: God was not made, but God the Son of God was born, and afterward made man from Mary according to the flesh. 'God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law': 'his Son' signifies the property of eternal generation, 'made of a woman' ascribes making to the assumption of a body, 'under the Law' to observance of the Law. One generation does not prejudice the other, nor flesh the divinity; the eternal God is one in both, not one from the Father and another from the Virgin, but the same in different ways: first-born because none before him, only-begotten because none after him.
claims: Christ was made from Mary according to the flesh, not as God.
He is one and the same, born differently of the Father and of the Virgin.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e179.summary: Concludes that these texts teach how to understand 'Christ was made', whether simply or with an addition: being made or being a creature is referred not to God assuming but to the man assumed.
claims: Being made refers to the man assumed, not to God.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e183.summary: Supports this with Ambrose: was Christ made by a word or created by a command? How can there be a creature in God, whose nature is simple, not joined or composite, to whom nothing accrues and who has only what is divine in his nature?
claims: There can be no creature in God.
God's nature is simple and admits no accidents.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e195.summary: Warns that though Christ according to man is called a creature, he is not to be predicated a creature simply. Nor can one argue: if Christ as man is a creature, it is either rational or not, God or not, so as to prove that Christ is something non-divine, on the ground that what he is as man, he is.
claims: Christ is not simply predicated a creature.
One cannot infer that Christ is something non-divine.

pl-l3d11c2-d1e198.summary: Explains why: right argument does not proceed from figurative locutions, and calling Christ a creature, simply or with an addition, is figurative.
claims: Calling Christ a creature is figurative speech.
Valid arguments do not proceed from figurative statements.

pl-l3d11c2.summary: Recalls Arius's perfidy in confessing Christ a creature and his gruesome death. From these testimonies Christ should not be called made or a creature simply, but with a qualification, 'made according to the flesh' or 'according to the man', so that being made is attributed to the humanity, not to God (Ambrose on Gal 4:4). There can be no creature in God, whose nature is simple. And though Christ according to man is a creature, one cannot argue from this that Christ is something non-divine, since such statements are figurative and figurative speech does not support valid arguments.
claims: Christ may be called made only with the qualification 'according to the flesh'.
Being made is attributed to the humanity assumed, not to God assuming.
There can be no creature in God.
One cannot argue validly from figurative statements.
